brief.head: Keep the yolk
brief.text: Dietary choles­terol has noth­ing to do with the choles­terol in our body, Amit Varma said, call­ing the egg yolk per­haps the health­i­est food known to man. {009-C07}

brief.head: Salad, then dessert
brief.text: Eating order mat­ters, Amit Varma found: fibre first, pro­tein sec­ond, carbs last. The Western meal of salad, main course and dessert turns out to be ideal. {009-C10}

brief.head: A better atta
brief.text: Ajay Shah pitched food pro­ces­sors an idea: split whole wheat, set aside 10 units of the maida, re­com­bine, and sell a su­pe­rior atta with a built-in dis­count. {009-C21}

brief.head: Buffet in a bottle
brief.text: Multivitamins are “kinda like a five-star buf­fet”, said Amit Varma, pass­ing on his nu­tri­tion­ist friend Shruti Jahagirdar’s ad­vice. Work out what you lack and take that in­stead. {009-C20}

brief.head: Remember the Emergency
brief.text: Recommending Coomi Kapoor’s *The Emergency*[[x3]], Amit Varma ar­gued it was no aber­ra­tion: India’s con­sti­tu­tion cen­tralised power[[x4]], and a dom­i­nant state is in the Indian state’s DNA. {009-C22}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma on how he reversed his type 2 diabetes
lead.head: Reversed, one meal a day

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 9

body: Amit Varma’s doc­tor pre­scribed met­formin and the usual drugs. When Varma asked about diet, the doc­tor looked em­bar­rassed and said only: “You’re a smart man, you know what to do.” {009-S08}
Varma sensed, he said, that the doc­tor knew ev­ery­thing he had been taught was wrong but could not say so.
In fact Varma did know. He had read the books and gifted Jason Fung’s *The Diabetes Code* to friends. “Intellectually I knew, but I was too lazy,” he said.

What closed the gap was a sen­sor on the arm. His co-host Ajay Shah sug­gested a con­tin­u­ous glu­cose mon­i­tor, or CGM, and Varma watched in real time what each meal did to his blood. Guided by it, he moved to keto and then to one meal a day, and his HbA1c fell from 7.7 to 5.7.
“It is re­versible, type 2 di­a­betes[[x1]], it can be re­versed through diet alone,” Varma said. “It is a dis­ease of the diet.” {009-C05}
Any doc­tor who says oth­er­wise, he added, is “a lying quack”.
## A hor­mone, not a help­ing

The episode’s back­bone was Gary Taubes’s *The Case Against Sugar*. Taubes ar­gues that sug­ars cause di­a­betes and obe­sity in the same sense that cig­a­rettes cause lung can­cer: through their hor­monal ef­fects, not be­cause we eat too much. {009-C01}
Sugar, Varma said, hits the brain’s re­ward cen­tre like nico­tine or al­co­hol, yet we never feel with­drawal, be­cause we are never with­out it for long.
Every meal brings an in­sulin spike, and fre­quent spikes push the body to­wards in­sulin re­sis­tance. So small fre­quent meals, a dietitian’s sta­ple, “are ter­ri­ble”, he said.
## How the dogma set
Why were we told oth­er­wise? Varma traced a cen­tury of error, from a physi­cian who blamed the motor car to a sugar lobby that Franklin Roosevelt could not beat.

The turn­ing point was Ancel Keys, whose Seven Countries Study blamed sat­u­rated fat for heart dis­ease. Keys, Varma said, cherry-picked his coun­tries, and by 1961 the American Heart Association was urg­ing low-fat diets. {009-S04}
Varma called what the sugar lobby did “a far greater scan­dal” than any­thing the to­bacco lobby did.
He did not spare the peo­ple be­hind it. When he thinks of Keys or the prom­i­nent peo­ple in the sugar lobby, he said, “I think of them as men who com­mit­ted crimes on hu­man­ity.”
## Know thy­self

Shah, who has worn a CGM for his own ex­per­i­ments, re­framed the les­son. We are usu­ally handed a diet, he said, when we should start from our own tastes and food cul­ture and adapt them to our bod­ies. {009-C08}

His find­ings were pre­cise. Sugar be­haves dif­fer­ently alone, with fat and with spices. White rice and maida are “merely poly­merised sug­ars”. And a calo­rie is not a calo­rie: com­plex carbs feed the mi­crobes in the gut, which eat some of the en­ergy.
Varma urged scep­ti­cism of nu­tri­tion stud­ies, whose fun­ders de­serve scru­tiny while the sugar lobby re­mains pow­er­ful.
Varma did not want to sell any­one a diet. “Why should you lis­ten to me?” he asked. Read the books, he said, get a CGM and fig­ure out what works for you.
His clos­ing ad­vice came in two parts: “One, know thy­self and two, sugar is poi­son.”

second.label: The fat theory
second.head: Keys to a bad diet
second.deck: How one study’s choice of countries turned America against fat

pic.caption: Ancel Keys at a press conference in Gioia Tauro, Italy, in 1960

body: In the late 1950s Ancel Keys pub­lished his Seven Countries Study, which ap­peared to link sat­u­rated fat with heart dis­ease[[x2]].

Amit Varma called it “deeply in­tel­lec­tu­ally dis­hon­est”. To test a hy­poth­e­sis, he said, you must ex­am­ine what­ever could dis­prove it. Keys left out France, with its high-fat diet and low heart dis­ease, as well as Switzerland and Germany. His cho­sen coun­tries also ate a lot of sugar, which he skipped over. {009-S04}

The American Heart Association ar­gued against him in 1957. By 1960 he sat on its main panel, and in 1961 it is­sued low-fat guide­lines. Obesity, Varma said, went from about one in seven Americans to one in three over the next forty years. {#obesity}

quote.text: He cherry picks the coun­tries, then he cherry picks the ev­i­dence, then he comes to the con­clu­sion that fat is the prob­lem.

third.head: How sugar lit a Camel

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the sweetened Camel

body: Until 1913, cig­a­rette smoke was al­ka­line, Amit Varma said, so any­one who tried to in­hale it would start cough­ing. {009-S02}

That year a new brand, Camel, ar­rived. Its mak­ers raised the car­bo­hy­drate con­tent of the to­bacco, and so its sugar. The smoke turned acidic, be­came easy to in­hale, and be­came more ad­dic­tive.

“I would say that in a sense, sug­ars en­abled smok­ing to cause lung can­cer,” Varma said. He had the his­tory from Gary Taubes’s *The Case Against Sugar*, which he called the best over­ar­ch­ing look at the sub­ject. {009-R01}

Varma found sugar’s pull summed up in Michael Pollan’s *The Botany of Desire*. Pollan de­scribes his son Isaac’s first taste of birth­day-cake icing and imag­ines him ex­claim­ing: “Your world con­tains this. From this day on­wards I shall ded­i­cate my life to it.” {009-J10}

p2.title: Sugar on trial
p2.deck: How sugar escaped blame for a century, and what a sensor on the arm reveals

quote.text: We will never ex­pe­ri­ence a with­drawal symp­tom be­cause we are never with­out sugar for long enough to ex­pe­ri­ence that with­drawal symp­tom.

photo.caption: Gary Taubes presenting at the Ancestral Health Symposium in 2012

box.title: The case for the prosecution
box.text: Gary Taubes, an award-winning sci­ence jour­nal­ist, ar­gues that sugar causes di­a­betes and obe­sity the way smok­ing causes lung can­cer. Amit Varma called *The Case Against Sugar* the best over­ar­ch­ing look at the sub­ject, and for him the most de­fin­i­tive. {009-R01}

sections.label: The charge
sections.head: Worse than a sweet tooth
sections.caption: sugar’s hormonal harm
body: Amit Varma began with a read­ing list: Sidney Mintz’s *Sweetness and Power*, Nina Teicholz’s *The Big Fat Surprise*, and Jason Fung’s *The Obesity Code* and *The Diabetes Code*. {009-R05}

But the key book, he said, was Gary Taubes’s *The Case Against Sugar*[[x6]]. Michael Pollan once called Taubes “a Solzhenitsyn of the nu­tri­tion world”, for tak­ing on dog­mas from the late 1990s on. {009-J09}

Taubes ar­gues that sug­ars such as su­crose and high-fructose corn syrup cause di­a­betes and obe­sity in the same sense that smok­ing causes lung can­cer, “not be­cause we eat too much of these sug­ars”, but through their hor­monal ef­fects. {009-C01}
## A slow-acting poi­son

They are not short-term tox­ins, Taubes writes, but do their dam­age over years and decades, per­haps even from gen­er­a­tion to gen­er­a­tion, through what moth­ers eat and how that changes the womb[[x7]].

Varma calls sugar the most ad­dic­tive sub­stance out there. It acts on the brain’s re­ward cen­tre as nico­tine and al­co­hol do. Too much cof­fee leaves you jit­tery; sugar gives no such warn­ing. And since we are never with­out it, we never feel with­drawal. {009-C02}

~ The charge sheet runs on. Varma linked sugar to hy­per­ten­sion and heart dis­ease, said re­searchers are study­ing its links with can­cer, and noted that some call Alzheimer’s dis­ease “type 3 di­a­betes”.

quote.text: We will never ex­pe­ri­ence a with­drawal symp­tom be­cause we are never with­out sugar for long enough to ex­pe­ri­ence that with­drawal symp­tom.

sections.label: The history
sections.head: Blame it on the motor car
sections.caption: the motor car and other suspects
body: In 1907 Kailas Chunder Bose, “a fel­low Bengali” of Amit Varma’s, ob­served that with pros­per­ity under British rule, “the num­ber of di­a­betic cases has enor­mously in­creased.” {009-J11}

Early physi­cians linked di­a­betes to car­bo­hy­drates. But Elliott Joslin, who be­came America’s most prom­i­nent di­a­betes physi­cian, looked else­where. In 1925 he said au­to­mo­biles cause di­a­betes: peo­ple stopped walk­ing, got fat, then got di­a­betes.
His ally Harold Himsworth wrote a paper, now known to be flawed, blam­ing fat. Meanwhile Prohibition pushed Americans from al­co­hol to candy, and sugar con­sump­tion soared.

Nobody joined the dots, Varma said. Physicians un­der­stood hor­mones but not diet; nu­tri­tion­ists lacked the med­i­cal in­sight. So other the­o­ries took root, “then ca­bals build along those the­o­ries, ca­reers are based on those the­o­ries”. {009-S03}
## Wealth, or cul­ture?
Ajay Shah asked whether all this was sim­ply in­come elas­tic­ity. Partly, Varma said, but Japan, France and Germany grew pros­per­ous with­out the same re­sult. Culture mat­tered too.

He re­called the Dalit scholar Chandra Bhan Prasad, whose obese, di­a­betic vil­lage el­ders fill him with pride: a cou­ple of gen­er­a­tions ago, they would not have been pros­per­ous enough to get di­a­betes. {009-S06}
~ Prasad says much the same of the ghung­hat. Lower-caste women were not al­lowed to wear it, so a Dalit bride who wears one is ex­er­cis­ing a choice she was once de­nied.

quote.text: When I go back to my vil­lage and I see my vil­lage el­ders are obese and they have di­a­betes, my heart fills with pride.
quote.who: Chandra Bhan Prasad, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: The lobby
sections.head: Fat framed, sugar walks
sections.caption: the sugar lobby
body: By the 1930s, Amit Varma said, two dog­mas were form­ing: that fat causes chronic dis­eases such as heart dis­ease, and that obe­sity is sim­ply calo­ries in ex­ceed­ing calo­ries out.

The sugar lobby[[x8]], mean­while, grew mighty. Franklin Roosevelt called it the most pow­er­ful in­ter­est group he had seen. “This is a man who won World War II in a sense,” Varma said, “but couldn’t beat the sugar lobby.” {009-J13}

Critics were bru­tally shut down. In 1976 Jean Mayer wrote a *New York Times* piece about the bit­ter truth of sugar. *Reader’s Digest* planned to run ex­cerpts until calls were made to its man­ag­ing ed­i­tor, and it was spiked. {009-S05}

In 1977 the US Senate’s di­etary goals[[x9]] rec­om­mended a low-fat diet and said sugar was per­fectly fine. On a chart from Nina Teicholz’s book, Varma said, American obe­sity shoots up from around then.
## Why the myth sur­vives

The push­back con­tin­ues from three sources, he said: cor­po­rate in­ter­ests hid­ing sugar be­hind la­bels such as “no added sugar”; Paul Graham’s “ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional minded”; and self-interested de­fend­ers of the sta­tus quo, in­clud­ing doc­tors trained the wrong way. {009-C04}
~ In India, he warned, going to a doc­tor over forty is dan­ger­ous un­less they have kept up­dat­ing them­selves. If you grad­u­ated in 2010 or even a lit­tle later, “chances are you’re wrong.”

quote.text: It’s hard to imag­ine now the heat of the pas­sion. It was just like we had des­e­crated the American flag.
quote.who: David Kritchevsky, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: The sensor
sections.head: Your blood, in real time
sections.caption: his time in range
body: Ajay Shah, who had sug­gested the CGM[[x10]] to Amit Varma, put the les­son his own way. We are usu­ally handed a diet, he said; we should in­stead start from our own tastes and food cul­ture, and adapt them until they work for our bod­ies. {009-C08}

HbA1c, he said, is a smeared av­er­age of three months of blood sugar. A CGM shows the pic­ture mo­ment by mo­ment, so surges and volatil­ity be­come vis­i­ble. His rule of thumb is to stay be­tween 70 and 160 for over 80 per cent of the day, and never below 70. {009-C09}
## What sugar keeps com­pany with

Shah tested one dose of sugar alone, with fat, and with fat plus spices such as gin­ger, nut­meg and cin­na­mon. Each pro­duced a dif­fer­ent surge. If you must have sugar, he said, make it ice cream, ide­ally spiced. {009-C11}
Simple starches are no refuge. A hun­dred grams of white rice, he said, is “pretty much the same” as a hun­dred grams of sugar, one re­ac­tion with the en­zyme amy­lase away. {009-C12}
A CGM is ex­pen­sive, but habits form in two or three months, so Shah sug­gested two or three rig­or­ous months on one each year. {009-C13}
~ Food is so­cial, he added. If there is cheese­cake in the fridge it will end up in­side you, so change what the house­hold buys, even if that means being “rude”.

quote.text: We should try to stay be­tween 70 and 160 for over 80 per­cent of the day.

sections.label: The gut
sections.head: The microbes take their cut
sections.caption: the gut microbiome
body: Calorie counts come from burn­ing food in pure oxy­gen, Ajay Shah said, and that may not be how the body pro­cesses it.

He began with plants. In hy­dro­pon­ics[[x11]], plants fed sim­ple chem­i­cal fer­tiliser un­der­in­vest in their root mi­cro­biome, and lose nu­tri­tional qual­ity and the abil­ity to fight dis­ease. {009-C16}
Simple carbs, he said, do the same to us. They are ab­sorbed soon after the stom­ach, so the gut mi­cro­biome is not fed and shriv­els. Complex carbs travel all the way down and feed it.

A paper by Corbin and col­leagues in *Nature Communications* in June 2023 com­pared diets with iden­ti­cal calo­ries. On some mea­sures the gut mi­cro­biome was 8x higher on com­plex carbs, and the mi­crobes ate some of the en­ergy: a dif­fer­ence of about 200 calo­ries a day. {009-C15}
## Read the label, and the study
Labels mis­lead, Amit Varma warned. Shah named one stan­dard trick, con­cen­trated apple juice: “a way of get­ting sugar in and say­ing this is hun­dred per­cent fruit”.
Varma urged read­ers to check who funded a nu­tri­tion study and how it was done, and to trust meta-studies over sin­gle ones. {009-C19}
~ Told that a glass of wine is good for the heart, Varma asked what it does to the liver. Shah added that stud­ies show the best amount of al­co­hol is zero.

quote.text: Look at each study with a de­fault po­si­tion of being crit­i­cal of it and then fig­ur­ing out what’s going on there.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the gut microbiome

quote.text: In the world of diet, we are nor­mally told, here’s a diet. Whereas what we should be ask­ing is where are my pref­er­ences? And what are my tastes and what is my food cul­ture?

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Poker, a mountain, a chess rating and a boss who made people cry

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how he gained, lost and regained the weight
stories.head: Dealt a bad hand at 107 kg
body: Amit Varma spent five years as a pro­fes­sional poker player. It paid bet­ter than any­thing else he could have done, he said, but it was cor­ro­sive as a life­style: “You play a 15-hour ses­sion, go home and sleep, play an­other 15-hour ses­sion.” {#poker}

About five or six years be­fore the episode, when he dis­cov­ered the books, he weighed 105 kg. He read them, took up keto with in­ter­mit­tent fast­ing, ran every day, and lost about 20 kg. At 85 or 86 kg he was full of en­ergy, even ran a 10k, and held that weight for a long time.

Then COVID made him seden­tary. Whenever he needed com­fort, it was biryani or pizza. “It’s just one meal,” he said. “And so one meal at a time, I went in the wrong di­rec­tion, went to 107.” {009-S07}
About 18 months be­fore the episode he was di­ag­nosed with type 2 di­a­betes and hy­per­ten­sion, with an HbA1c of 7.7. Three months on met­formin changed lit­tle.
Then Ajay Shah sug­gested a con­tin­u­ous glu­cose mon­i­tor. Varma wore one through three two-week cy­cles. A slice of toast sent his glu­cose to 285; eggs and bacon left a flat line.

He moved to keto and in­ter­mit­tent fast­ing, then to one meal a day, eaten be­tween six and eight after cook­ing two- or three-course din­ners to music. He calls it a re­ally happy pe­riod. His HbA1c fell from 7.7 to 5.7. {#hba1c}
~ He is now at around 95 kg, no longer on keto, and plans to reach 85 be­fore set­tling into in­ter­mit­tent fast­ing with low carbs.
stories.why: Knowing is not doing. Varma had gifted *The Diabetes Code* to friends while stay­ing too lazy to act. Seeing his own body’s re­sponse closed the gap, and con­vinced him type 2 di­a­betes is “a dis­ease of the diet”. {009-C05}
stories.postscript: A friend who swore by oats tried a CGM: oats took her to 280, eggs flat­lined, and she lost 25 kg. {009-S09}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on reversing his own diabetes

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s CGM, on a hike near Dharamshala
stories.head: A summit meal in three acts
body: A month or two be­fore the episode, Ajay Shah was hik­ing in the hills near Dharamshala, wear­ing a CGM[[x12]]. At the top he had a 500 ml bot­tle of Gatorade, white rice and rajma.
Then he walked con­tin­u­ously down­hill for 1,000 me­tres. {#descend} Eaten on the plains, he said, such a meal would bring an in­dis­tinct mess of a surge, el­e­vated for hours.

Burning en­ergy fast, he in­stead saw “three dis­tinct surges”, each burned off in turn: first the Gatorade’s sugar, then the white rice as amy­lase turned it into sugar, and last the rajma’s com­plex carbs. {009-S10}
~ “I vividly saw what they tell us in the books,” Shah said: sim­ple sugar reaches the blood im­me­di­ately, while com­plex carbs take their time.
stories.why: Everyday life smears over­lap­ping sig­nals to­gether and hides cause and ef­fect. On an empty stom­ach and a steep de­scent, the text­book tim­ing of sugar, starch and com­plex carbs be­came vis­i­ble. Shah stressed that he does not rec­om­mend the meal.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma ad­mit­ted the story made him crave rajma, “de­spite the windy things it does to you the next morn­ing”.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) on the three surges, with Amit Varma

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on sugar, brain fog and bullet chess
stories.head: A pizza costs 150 points
body: One side ef­fect of sugar that Amit Varma had not yet men­tioned is brain fog. Off keto, he said, he tires sooner and thinks far worse. {#fog}

He has an ob­jec­tive mea­sure. He plays bul­let chess on chess.com[[x13]], a whole bunch of games every day, under a pseu­do­nym: “no one shall ever know.” He plays as an ad­dict, not to im­prove, so his rat­ing holds steady.
On keto, it climbs about 150 points. After a cheat day with pizza, it drops about 150, “or even more if I add a biryani to the pizza”. {009-S11}
~ Pizza plus biryani, Varma said, is a lit­tle like Louis CK’s “bang bang”: one com­plete meal in one restau­rant, then straight into an­other with a dif­fer­ent cui­sine for an­other com­plete meal.
stories.why: Sugar’s cost to clear think­ing is real, and it can be mea­sured. Any ac­tiv­ity done con­sis­tently every day can serve as a per­sonal gauge of how well the mind is work­ing.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on his chess rating

stories.kicker: A former colleague’s verdict on Ajay Shah
stories.head: The monster they returned to
body: The day be­fore record­ing, Amit Varma met a for­mer col­league of Ajay Shah’s, who spent four years with him at the fi­nance min­istry and many years at the UN.
Shah, she said, was hor­ri­ble to work with, “a mon­ster”. “He would make me cry,” she said, and it hap­pened to ev­ery­one. “But we al­ways used to come back and work with him again.” {009-S01}

Why? Because they learnt so much, she said, and learnt how to learn. Put to Shah, the charge drew an economist’s an­swer: “The most in­ter­est­ing stuff in life is just the in­vis­i­ble spillovers that are not in­ter­me­di­ated by the mar­ket sys­tem.” {009-C18}

~ We are each a lin­ear com­bi­na­tion of our in­flu­ences[[x14]], Shah said, and im­pose ex­ter­nal­i­ties on one an­other, some­times pos­i­tive, some­times neg­a­tive. All the good stuff in the world, he added, hap­pens like that.
stories.why: Demanding men­tors hurt at the time and trans­form peo­ple later. Shah calls such in­flu­ence an ex­ter­nal­ity: un­priced, in­vis­i­ble, and in his view the place where most of the good in the world hap­pens.
stories.postscript: Varma’s reply: “I keep telling my writ­ing stu­dents, don’t use jar­gon, don’t use jar­gon. Look what you just did.” {009-J02}

quiz.q: What did Camel’s makers change in 1913, and why did that matter to smokers?
quiz.a: They raised the sugar con­tent, so the smoke turned acidic, in­hal­able and more ad­dic­tive.

quiz.q: Which high-fat, low-heart-disease country did Ancel Keys leave out of his famous study?
quiz.a: France, along with Switzerland and Germany, which could have dis­proved his hy­poth­e­sis.

quiz.q: What happened when Amit Varma’s oat-loving friend finally wore a CGM?
quiz.a: Oats sent her glu­cose to 280, eggs flat­lined, and she lost 25 kg.

quiz.q: Within what band does Ajay Shah aim to keep his blood sugar, and how often?
quiz.a: Between 70 and 160, for over 80 per cent of the day.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, do complex carbs earn a calorie discount?
quiz.a: They reach the gut mi­cro­biome, and the mi­crobes eat some of the en­ergy.

quiz.q: What does Amit Varma use as an objective measure of his brain fog?
quiz.a: His bul­let-chess rat­ing, which climbs about 150 points on keto and falls after pizza.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 9. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Joslin (Joslin.org, public domain); Michael Pollan (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); David Remnick (Martin Schneider / en:User:Priceyeah, CC BY-SA 2.5). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Open Library and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: The Case Against Sugar
shelf.creator: Gary Taubes
shelf.why: In Amit’s view it gives the best over­ar­ch­ing ac­count of the sub­ject.

shelf.title: The Big Fat Surprise
shelf.creator: Nina Teicholz
shelf.why: It shows how the low-fat dogma and the Ancel Keys era mis­led a gen­er­a­tion, and how dis­senters were si­lenced.

shelf.title: The Obesity Code
shelf.creator: Jason Fung
shelf.why: Part of the core read­ing that con­vinced Amit that the stan­dard di­etary wis­dom on weight is wrong.

shelf.title: The Diabetes Code
shelf.creator: Jason Fung
shelf.why: It lays out how type 2 di­a­betes can be re­versed through diet, which is the premise of the whole episode.

shelf.title: Sweetness and Power
shelf.creator: Sidney Mintz
shelf.why: It pro­vides the his­tor­i­cal ground­ing for un­der­stand­ing sugar’s hold on us.

shelf.title: The Botany of Desire
shelf.creator: Michael Pollan
shelf.why: It cap­tures, bet­ter than any statis­tic, how in­tox­i­cat­ing and ad­dic­tive sugar is from the very first taste.

shelf.title: Nina Teicholz on The Joe Rogan Experience
shelf.creator: Joe Rogan, Nina Teicholz
shelf.why: An ac­ces­si­ble entry point to Teicholz’s case for read­ers not ready for the book.

shelf.title: The perfect treatment for diabetes and weight loss (Jason Fung interviewed by Diet Doctor)
shelf.creator: Jason Fung
shelf.why: It ex­plains why fre­quent eat­ing means fre­quent in­sulin spikes and moves you to­ward in­sulin re­sis­tance.

shelf.title: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (Episode 296 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma, Chandra Bhan Prasad
shelf.why: The Dalit thinker whose two he­roes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith, a pair­ing cen­tral to Amit’s hope for end­ing caste.

shelf.title: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Paul Graham’s two-axis map of thinkers (con­ven­tional or in­de­pen­dent, pas­sive or ag­gres­sive) that sin­gles out the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded as the loud­est voices and the real ob­sta­cle to new ideas.

shelf.title: Ajay speaks out against Hydroponics
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s anti-recommendation: hy­dro­ponic leaves look clean, but grow­ing plants in water starves their root mi­cro­biome and leaves them nu­tri­tion­ally in­fe­rior, so pre­fer plants grown in healthy soil.

shelf.title: Host-diet-gut microbiome interactions influence human energy balance
shelf.creator: Karen D Corbin et al.
shelf.why: It com­pared diets with iden­ti­cal calo­ries and found that com­plex carbs feed the gut mi­cro­biome, which con­sumes some of the en­ergy.

shelf.title: Are all calories created equal? Your gut microbes don’t think so.
shelf.creator: Anahad O’Connor
shelf.why: A read­able news­pa­per ac­count (Washington Post) of the gut-microbiome calo­rie find­ings.

shelf.title: FreeStyle Libre Glucose Monitoring System (Reader & Sensor)
shelf.creator: Abbott Labs
shelf.why: It is the CGM that made this whole jour­ney pos­si­ble.

shelf.title: Shruti Jahagirdar (nutritionist and physical trainer)
shelf.why: She de­signs a com­plete plan around your body weight and goals, ad­vises veg­e­tar­i­ans on keto, and be­lieves in re­sis­tance train­ing.

shelf.title: Shruti Jahagirdar is the Sporty One (Episode 289 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma, Shruti Jahagirdar
shelf.why: A way to get to know her ap­proach be­fore con­sult­ing her.

shelf.title: The Emergency: A Personal History
shelf.creator: Coomi Kapoor
shelf.why: A journalist’s first-hand ac­count of the Emergency, when half the op­po­si­tion and hordes of jour­nal­ists were jailed and a ster­il­i­sa­tion drive spun out of con­trol.

shelf.title: Coomi Kapoor Has the Inside Track (Episode 305 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma, Coomi Kapoor
shelf.why: A long con­ver­sa­tion with Coomi Kapoor, whose first-hand ac­count of the Emergency Amit re­lies on; a com­pan­ion to her book The Emergency: A Personal History.

shelf.title: Gyan Prakash on the Emergency (Episode 103 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma, Gyan Prakash
shelf.why: It frames the Emergency as part of the Indian state’s cen­tral­is­ing DNA, in­her­ited from the colo­nial state.

shelf.title: Lenin’s Tomb: The Last Days of the Soviet Empire
shelf.creator: David Remnick
shelf.why: It shows how a so­ci­ety strug­gles with an au­thor­i­tar­ian state and how progress is dam­aged for a very long time.

shelf.title: The Bridge: The Life and Rise of Barack Obama
shelf.creator: David Remnick
shelf.why: Full of re­veal­ing de­tail, in­clud­ing the trivia that Obama played poker to net­work with Democratic Party in­sid­ers.

shelf.title: Louie
shelf.creator: Louis CK
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great show, and the bit per­fectly names his pizza-plus-biryani binges.

laughs.text: The nam­ing joke that opens the show: ‘We just thought that we could call this show Amit and Shah. Because you know, Amit and Shah. But we’re not gonna do that.’ (The pun is on a prom­i­nent politician’s name.)

After Ajay an­swers the ‘you made peo­ple cry’ charge in eco­nom­ics-speak about ex­ter­nal­i­ties, Amit says: ‘You know, I keep telling my writ­ing stu­dents, don’t use jar­gon, don’t use jar­gon. Look what you just did.’

On Ajay’s line that cheese­cake in the fridge ends up in­side you, Amit adds: ‘If there is a choice of the cheese­cake being in­side you and you being in­side the cheese­cake, please choose the sec­ond op­tion. Even if it is hard to imag­ine and a lit­tle bit messy and you’ll need a good shower later. Midjourney, here we come... Ajay Shah in­side a cheese­cake.’
Amit on rajma: ‘Who doesn’t love Rajma? Despite the windy things it does to you the next morn­ing.’

Amit on doc­tors who call type 2 di­a­betes ir­re­versible: ‘any doc­tor who tells you type 2 di­a­betes is a chronic dis­ease and can­not be re­versed is a lying quack. Treat him as no bet­ter than a home­o­pathic doc­tor or an Ayurvedic doc­tor.’

Amit trips over his Obama trivia: ‘Barack Obama was also just like me.’ Ajay: ‘A bas­ket­ball player.’ Amit: ‘I’m not a bas­ket­ball player. Barack Obama, just like me, was also a poker player.’ He then weighs the trade-off: ‘You avoid sugar but you get gam­bling. I don’t know which is a big­ger evil... I didn’t get type two di­a­betes by play­ing poker, so we know what the an­swer to that is.’

The sign-off pitch: pro­ducer Vartika says Ajay needs pat­terned shirts, since he is down to the plain white ones he wears every day. So Ajay has been telling friends, ‘guys, gift me shirts.’ Amit: ‘We want shirts, but like and sub­scribe.’
Michael Pollan once de­scribed Gary Taubes as ‘a Solzhenitsyn of the nu­tri­tion world’, for tak­ing on nu­tri­tion or­tho­doxy.
Pollan in The Botany of Desire, on his son Isaac’s first taste of birth­day-cake icing, imag­ined as say­ing: ‘Your world con­tains this. From this day on­wards I shall ded­i­cate my life to it.’

Kailas Chunder Bose, 1907: ‘There is not the slight­est shadow of a doubt that with the progress of civ­i­liza­tion, of high ed­u­ca­tion, and in­creased wealth and pros­per­ity of the peo­ple under the British rule, the num­ber of di­a­betic cases has enor­mously in­creased.’
Franklin Roosevelt called the sugar lobby the most pow­er­ful in­ter­est group he had seen. Amit: ‘This is a man who won World War II in a sense, but couldn’t beat the sugar lobby.’
Amit in­vokes The Insider, a film about the to­bacco lobby, and calls what the sugar lobby did ‘a far greater scandal’.

Louis CK’s ‘bang bang’ from Louie: eat a com­plete meal at one restau­rant, walk straight into an­other restau­rant serv­ing a dif­fer­ent cui­sine, and eat an­other com­plete meal. Amit’s pizza-plus-biryani counts.
L.K. Advani on the press dur­ing the Emergency: they were asked to bend, and they chose to crawl.
